newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU concerned about industry competitiveness.
newsitem.headline: EU concerned about industry competitiveness.

text.p: European Union industry ministers agreed at the weekend on the need to improve the competitiveness of Europe's industry which is lagging behind that of economic rivals the United States and Japan.
The informal Industry Council debated what could be done to boost the position of the bloc's business sectors.

"There was complete agreement among industry ministers that we should work much more systematically on the issue of European competitiveness, that we should focus more on the high growth areas," said Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers.
"There are clear signals that we have to improve European competitiveness," he told reporters, adding that there was "absolutely reason to be worried."
Figures from the European Commission show that the EU has managed to create only 10 million new jobs since the 1960s, less than one fifth of what the United States has achieved.

As a result, the EU unemployment rate stands at 11 percent compared with about 5.5 percent in the United States. In addition, the EU level of gross domestic product per capita is nearly one third below that of the United States.

"Those are examples that we have to study, how we organise our economies, because that is the only way to solve the issue of unemployment, to see that our competitive position vis-a-vis the other important economic powers improves," Wijers said.
He said he was pleased with the general "sense of urgency" at the session, which like other informal ministerial EU meetings did not take any concrete decisions.

A study by consultancy Booz-Allen&Hamilton, commissioned by the Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs, highlighted the problems, showing that Europe is falling behind in crucial information and communication technology (ICT) industries.

The study, which was presented during the ministerial meeting, calls for "dramatically accelerated" reform to help boost Europe's ICT industries, which are seen as vital for creating future jobs and economic growth.

"On the whole the European ICT industries lag behind competitors in most sectors in the United States and to a lesser extent in Asia," Gerd Wittkemper, senior vice president of Booz-Allen&Hamilton, told a news conference on the sidelines of the meeting.
"It is obviously not a conscious decision, but Europe is letting opportunities for job creation slip between its fingers," he said.

EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said the bloc's single market had helped to create jobs, increased income and lowered inflation but that it was not yet fully implemented and had therefore far from "delivered its full potential".

To plug the gaps in the single market -- which took effect on January 1, 1993 -- the European Commission plans to put forward an action plan at the EU summit in Amsterdam in June. "That will indicate very specific concrete action...so as to achieve the single market in reality by the date of January 1, 1999," Monti said.
It would include proposals for action in the fields of taxation, services, simplification and enforcement of EU legislation.
However, Monti rejected any suggestion of a full harmonisation of national taxation systems. "That would not only be highly unrealistic but also in my view totally undesirable."
EU Industrial Affairs Commissioner Martin Bangemann said the EU's planned economic and monetary union -- due to start in 1999 -- would also help boost competitiveness.
